{"docket_number": "81-9", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1981", "first_party": "Washington", "first_party_label": "Appellant", "second_party": "Seattle School District No. 1", "second_party_label": "Appellee", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Appeal", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit", "argued": ["1982-03-22T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Does the statewide initiative violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

In 1978, a Seattle school district adopted a mandatory busing plan to integrate its schools. No court or administrative body found the district to be engaged in unlawful segregation. A statewide initiative adopted in 1978 mandated a neighborhood school policy. The policy provided for some exceptions including voluntary busing options and mandatory busing if so ordered by state or federal courts. The initiative blocked the implementation of Seattle's mandatory busing plan. School officials challenged the Washington government in federal court.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. The initiative reordered the educational decisionmaking process by moving the power over busing for purposes of integration to state control. The state explicitly employed "the racial nature of a decision to determine the decisionmaking process." This kind of state action places an unconstitutional burden on racial minorities within the governmental process.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Thank you, gentlemen. The case is submitted. We'll hear arguments next in Washington against Seattle's school district. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. color, caste, or sex, consistent with that constitutional mandate. No Washington school district has ever been held to have operated a de jure segregated school system. And throughout the history of the state, the policy of local school districts has been to assign students to their neighborhood schools. In 1977, however, the Seattle School District started a massive busing program which was not required by either the state or federal Constitution. Seattle's program effectively wiped out the traditional neighborhood school assignment policy in that city. It was in this context that the Washington voters in the following year enacted a law which is the subject of this appeal. Subject to the requirements of the Constitution, this law limits the ability of local school districts to require any public school student to attend a school other than that which is nearest or next nearest to the student's place of residence. Recognizing constitutional imperatives then, the Washington voters gave the legitimate policy of neighborhood school assignment a higher priority than the policy of racial balancing in public schools. The question before this court is whether the state and its voters can restrict the exercise of authority by school districts which are creatures of the state. The Washington state law defines basic education, determines the content, provides the funding, provides average salary levels for school district staffs, provides staff-student ratios, specifies the number of hours the teacher must spend in the classroom, makes available funding for district transportation, and prescribes a number of other matters relating to educational curriculum and staffing. Washington law also provides for interdistrict voluntary transfer programs to improve racial balance and state planning to assist school districts in developing programs to relieve racial isolation. State administrative law conditions construction grants on a determination by the superintendent of public instruction that the proposed construction would not create or aggravate racial balance within the districts. In short, the legislature in the state of Washington is a super school board. Local school boards simply follow state policy. The legislature and the voters, through the democratic initiative process and the ultimate source of authority for school districts, are the source of authority for school districts. The voters of our state chose to restrict the authority of school districts so as to preserve the historical practice of assigning students to nearby schools. The record in this case and previous opinions of this court indicate the importance of neighborhood schools for children and their parents, be they of minority or non-minority race, and the district court so found. Such benefits include, for example, increased community supported input, enhanced safety, reduced cost, and improved home-school relations. In this respect, I cannot improve on Justice Powell's discussion in the Keys case. In contrast, assignment and transportation of students beyond a nearby school will minimize such benefit both to minority and non-minority students. This policy of nearby schools was approved by a statewide electorate and enacted into law because the people believed that it was the best for all the school children in our state. It is a policy that by its own terms and by an interpretation which I have pledged the Office of Attorney General may not be used to thwart any plan to cure to jury segregation or any plan to correct the dual school system. We'll resume there at one o'clock, Mr. Attorney General. Attorney General, you may continue. Mr. Chief Justice, may I please the Court. If this Court upholds the validity of the initiative, what will not happen and what will happen? First, such a ruling will not sanction discrimination in Washington schools. It will not signify a retreat by this Court from the constitutional prohibition against jury segregation or a dual school system, and it will not cause the Seattle district to revert to a segregated system because that system has never been segregated. If this Court upholds the validity of Initiative 350, there will be at least eight school districts having five or more schools with minority enrollments in excess of the statewide average, which will not change student assignments at all. And this is because these schools are already balanced on a school-by-school basis through application of Washington's traditional neighborhood school policy. Further, if this Court upholds the validity of the initiative, there will be one appellee school district that will not change its assignment pattern and two school districts that must. The Tacoma School District will continue to use a voluntary and magnet school system to achieve racial balancing in its schools with no real changes in student assignments. The Pasco School District will have to stop mandatory busing of minority children only to distant parts of the Pasco School District. This will prompt a fairer approach to addressing racial balance, one that does not fall on minority children only. The Seattle School District will have to stop the mandatory busing of wholesale numbers of children, both minority and non-minority, from one end of the district to the other, unless there is a constitutional reason to do so. The matter of racial busing and distribution in the schools will be steadily and affirmatively affected by demographic changes in the district. I invite your review of the charts prepared by the Seattle School District, which reflect the dispersal of minority student residences throughout the district. Comparing the charts of 1976 with current trends will show how the residences of minority students are becoming more and more dispersed over the entire city. Further, the Seattle School District will be subject to state policies, which will encourage the district to use all available techniques to address racial balance in student assignments. Two judges on the Court of Appeals and the District Court judge have concluded that the policy of nearby schools must be struck down on the theory that it amounts to an impermissible legislative classification based on racial criteria, and the Court relies on Hunter v. Erikson and Lee v. Nyquips. We urge this Court's critical review of the lower court holding as being unsound. In applying Initiative 350 to actual practice, we see there is a classification as between students who qualify for mandatory assignment to a distant school for one set of reasons versus students who do not qualify. The set of reasons which qualify for mandatory distance assignment are health, safety, special education requirements, or because of unfit or inadequate conditions. These are not imposed along racial lines. Conversely, one can readily identify reasons being asserted by the school district or that might be asserted otherwise for mandatory distance student assignments which do not qualify under the terms of the initiative, such as filling up classrooms at the opposite end of the district, accommodating teaching staff, obtaining more transportation funding from the state, balancing of classroom size, or adjusting racial balance to a declared standard. And the fact that the initiative is silent on such asserted reasons for distant student assignments and therefore does not qualify them does not provide the basis for a court to infer there is a class which is racial in nature. As Judge Wright in the Ninth Circuit pointed out in his dissent, the initiative is a neutral law that must be analyzed in terms of its content. Initiative 350 is benign in its treatment of races and is clearly distinguishable from the kind of law that was struck down in Hunter v. Erickson. Mr. Attorney General, aside from this one, number 350, has a statewide initiative ever been used in the state of Washington to modify local school board decisions? Not to modify local school board decisions, Your Honor, but the use of the initiative is so commonplace that it ranges from authorizing the coloring of oleomargarine, which I recall as a youngster, to most recently a statewide initiative to control the expenditure of funds for power-generating plants. So it's hardly an election goes by without at least one or two significant initiatives being on the ballot. In the case of Hunter v. Erickson... Let me ask you one more question. Am I correct? The District Court here did find that the initiative was enacted for the sole purpose of preventing busing for racial desegregation. Is that correct? The Court concluded, I believe, Your Honor, that it was in response to the Seattle plan. Yes. Do you dispute that? No, Your Honor. We certainly agree that the Seattle plan is what galvanized the action that sparked the initiative, but we certainly indicate that statewide there would have been other reasoning on the part of the voters and additional reasons for passing the initiative. You have spoken of racial balance. From what source does that standard derive? What was the balance that was sought to be achieved? Your Honor, this is a varying term, and it's critical to the decision in the case, because the racial balance that is intended by the Seattle School District when they speak is the formula that they use, which can be a moving target depending on the demographic changes in the district from year to year. The district court apparently had a slightly different thought in mind in its findings when it talked about racial balance. Well, in your answer to Justice Blackmun, I had the feeling that you, at least you didn't answer, that opposition to racial balance is not equivalent to a discriminatory racial purpose. It isn't, is it? Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honor. I misspoke in leaving that impression, because I do not believe, and I think the evidence in the record suggests that it was not opposition to racial balance. Well, even if it was opposition to racial balance, is that equivalent to a discriminatory racial purpose? If you say I'm against voluntary racial balancing, is that it? Oh, no, it's not, Your Honor. I believe under the decisions of this court that it would not be. Well, did the district court find that the initiative was animated by a discriminatory racial purpose or only as an opposition to racial balance? The court, the district court concluded, Your Honor, that there was, that that was a motivating intent. Which was? Which was? That there was an intent. As I was saying, yes, Your Honor, it was concluded that that purpose was a, one of the factors. What purpose? All right, and that's important, Your Honor, because we're suggesting that the purpose that the court described, the district court, was not a significant factor. To hold the initiative invalid on this basis is like holding a law conscripting clerics invalid because an atheist voted for it. How did he describe the purpose, though? The purpose that the district court, Your Honor, had in mind, we believe, reading the memorandum opinion and the findings that there. The purpose was to contradict or rescind the Seattle plan. That's what he picks out. Well, what do you make of the district court's finding in his conclusions of law at page 826 of the jurisdictional statement, Conclusion 3-2, that a racially discriminatory intent or purpose was one of the factors which motivated the adoption of the initiative? All right, Your Honor, it's true that that's certainly what the court has found. That's a conclusion recited by the court and that the court had in mind nothing more than the fact that the initiative rescinded the Seattle school plan. Now, the Court of Appeals didn't review that finding, did it? No, Your Honor. What effect does that have on us? Well, Justice Marshall, it is important. It isn't important? It is important to distinguish between the kind of so-called discriminatory intent that the district court had in mind. There are different kinds of discriminatory intents? Well, we're suggesting that... Some are good and some are bad? No, Your Honor. I don't mean to imply that at all. Well, what do you mean? I'm suggesting that the use of the term discriminatory intent is inappropriate, an inappropriate label here, because what the court has in mind is rescinding the Seattle plan. And it's ironic that in the... Well, where do you find that? Because there's no finding of fact to support anything beyond that, Your Honor. It says a conclusion, then. It's a conclusion without any finding to support it. To the contrary, the evidence that was put into the record, which the court excluded from... In this case, the judge even lied on Washington against Davis and said that had been satisfied. Didn't it? On page 826. That was the assertion and the conclusion, Your Honor. However, we submit... Does that still stand? Certainly the case law, yes, Your Honor. Washington against Davis is applicable, but we don't believe it was applied by this district court judge correctly. We have said in several cases, have we not, that there is no constitutional requirement to achieve any particular racial balance. Has the court not said that? That's certainly correct, Your Honor. And as recently as the Spangler decision, a California case has been an instance of changing demographic circumstances, where the court found it wasn't necessary to keep adjusting and make adjustments. Well, apart from keeping adjustments, is there any constitutional requirement to achieve any particular racial balance in the first instance? Absolutely. Once dual schools are abolished? Your Honor, that's exactly the state of the law that this case is... Do you know what it says that the state can't do it? No, Your Honor. To the contrary, they... What happened there? I didn't hear your first words, sir. Did Seattle do it on its own? It wasn't forced to. They undertook, Your Honor, to achieve a socially desirable goal of achieving racial balance in the schools. And what we're suggesting here is... Don't they have a right to do that? Yes, they not only have a right, Your Honor, but they have a duty under the... Don't they have a right to do it without the interference of the state? Ah, that's the point, Your Honor, of the case, that... Well, if you're talking about states' rights, what do you mean? No, sir, we are not... Right of the state or the right of the community? No, we're not talking about states' rights, Your Honor. We're talking about this Seattle school district being a creature of the state. We're talking about the state of Washington legislature through its electorate being a super school board that has been setting policy in all of the various areas of administering schools for all these years. And that this was simply a discreet choice by the voters of the state of Washington to accommodate not only the desirable benefits of neighborhood schools or, as they said in the initiative, next nearest schools, together with the desirable benefits... That's not what the judge said. It said it was for the purpose of destroying the Seattle plan. That's what the judge found. Correct, Your Honor. And we're saying that the voters of the state of Washington made a more discreet choice in accommodating the benefits of neighborhood schools with achieving racially diverse student bodies. Well, why is the city objecting? It would be so much of a favor to the city. Why is the city objecting? Perhaps pride of authorship, Your Honor. But the point is that testimony from one of the Seattle superintendents, such as Dr. Moberly, indicated they were proceeding with a voluntary plan which they had started out with. And we submit, given time, using other techniques, could have achieved racial balance appropriately. Well, what your argument comes down to, I'll ask you, does it come down to this proposition that a school district can't have a policy or a program which is in conflict with the overall state mandate? Is that your argument? That's correct, Your Honor, that it is the prerogative of the state legislature to set policy in this area, as it has done in so many others. The initiative, we believe, is benign in its treatment of races and is clearly distinguishable from the kind of law that was struck down in Hunter against Erickson. In that case, the city charter amendment had placed a special voting burden on any ordinance dealing with racial, religious, or ancestral discriminant ordinances in housing. The Hunter case, of course, is not a school case. Nevertheless, on its face, we submit it does provide an example of an explicit, impermissible classification and, by contrast, demonstrates why Initiative 350 is valid. And the nice circuit court effectively acknowledged that Initiative 350 does not create an explicit classification based on race, but nevertheless hold that it implicitly creates this classification. Even the brief of the appellate ease. Could I ask you a question? I understand this program or this statute deals with it's a prohibition against mandatory busing. Supposing instead of a prohibition against mandatory busing, it were a prohibition against voluntary busing, which the students might volunteer to go to more distant schools because they wanted to attend schools and achieve racial balance and so forth. The students voluntarily and individually wanted to achieve the objectives that the school board sought to achieve here. And the statute was enacted saying, no, you can't do it. We'll have the same prohibition against voluntary transfers. Would that create a racial classification? Yes, very possibly it would, Your Honor, for a couple of reasons. For one thing, we're getting very close to the Lee against Nyquist situation where we had a flat prohibition against the consideration of race in making assignments. We do not have that here. Rather, we have an affirmative statement in favor of the benefits of neighborhood or near neighborhood. We have the same affirmative statement in my hypothetical statute. We prefer neighborhood schools as a matter of state policy for the same reasons you set forth here, and therefore we will not permit cross-district transfers, even on a voluntary basis. Why would one be more of a racial classification than the other, the Statue of God as opposed to my hypothetical? Well, let me answer, Your Honor. I believe, as your hypothetical applies to our case, it's critical that it be voluntary because we don't want a situation where the neighborhood population would be frozen in place. We need to have the ability for movement through magnet schools, through open enrollment programs, or other techniques. Why do you need that? It seemed to me that the state interest in having the children go to the neighborhood school might well be paramount, as it is here. Because, Your Honor, if we were frozen into place, that could be as discriminatory and prohibiting movement as it is. But as to the question whether it's a racial classification, that's what I'm addressing myself to, I don't see why whether it prohibits mandatory on the one hand or voluntary on the other. Why one is more of a racial classification than the other. Because, Your Honor, if the effect were such as to make it lead us to deduce that there was an animus on the part of this statute to act against one race or another, then we would be finding that there was a discriminatory intent, perhaps a classification that would make the statute unconstitutional. The difference is not, then, in terms of whether one's a racial classification and the other is not, but rather whether one supports an inference of racial intent and the other does not. That's your difference. Yes, Your Honor. But you would say they should be judged equally on the question whether they create a racial classification. Yes, that's correct, Your Honor. Mr. Attorney General, Initiative 350 doesn't purport to limit the power of any court, federal or state, to direct busing in connection with a desegregation plan, does it? No, Your Honor, it does not. The courts remain free. Absolutely. While I've interrupted you, would it be permissible under law in your state for all school boards to be abolished and the power they now exercise to be vested, say, in the Secretary of Education or perhaps a state commission? Yes, sir. That could have been a choice exercised by the legislature when it initially created a school system pursuant to the Constitution to have a completely different administrative structure than it has today. Instead of being a racial classification, the legislative classification created by Initiative 350, we believe, is analogous to the classification at issue in Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts against Feeney. In that case, this court rejected the argument that a Massachusetts statute, creating an absolute lifetime employment preference to veterans, classified persons on the basis of sex. This court noted that while the statute excluded significant numbers of women from preferred state jobs, it could not plausibly be explained only as a gender-based classification. Veteran status is not uniquely male, just as opposition to busing is not uniquely a white majority view, nor is support of busing exclusively a minority point of view. And with regard to the case now before the court, it must be said that adoption of a nearby school policy cannot be explained solely on racial grounds. Preference for nearby schools is not limited to the racial majority, and preference for mandatory busing to achieve racial balance is not limited to racial minorities. To the contrary, significant numbers of both classes lie on either side of the busing controversy. Even though there is not an explicit classification based on race contained in the initiative, it's relevant to consider the question of whether there is an intent to discriminate as has been suggested. And that case, we believe, is controlled by the case of Washington against Davis. In short, the voters in the state of Washington have struck an accommodation. The question before this court is whether, in striking that accommodation, our state may limit the authority of its local school districts, which are agents of the state itself, to require conduct which is otherwise constitutionally permissible. In our view, it may certainly do so. In Washington, the legislature defines basic education and determines its content. The legislature then provides its funding. It also prescribes salary levels for school district employees and even dictates the amount of time teachers may spend in classrooms. The legislature in Washington is a super school board. Local school boards simply follow state educational policy. The legislature in our state has made an additional policy choice in the field of education, one which by its own terms may never be used to thwart any attempt to cure the jury segregation, should that occur in Washington state. General Eikenberry, the solicitor general's brief, as I read it, says that even a law which is racially neutral on its face may violate the Equal Protection Clause if it causes a disproportionately adverse impact on a racial minority that can be traced to purposeful discrimination. We have in place here, I suppose, a factual determination by the trial court that at least there was some purposeful or intentional discrimination. Do you agree with the solicitor general's statement that I just read to you? We agree, your honor, that it could be, but would vary from the court's, from the honor's reading of the district court's opinion in order that there are not technically findings. There was a conclusion which I believe is dependent purely on the matter of rescinding the Seattle school plan. Okay, so you would propose that there is no factual finding of an intent to discriminate? That's correct, your honor. Do you believe that there is a disproportionately adverse impact as this court has defined how we look at that? No, absolutely, your honor. We do not. I would reserve the rest of my time if I may, your honor. I will. I'll spend my time speaking to this record and the findings in this case. One need look at no more than the plain language of Initiative 350 in the context in which it arose. Do you agree with the proposition that there is no constitutional requirement to achieve any particular racial balance? We certainly do. That's what the court said unanimously in Swan and in several cases thereafter. The Seattle plan does not require any particular degree of racial balance either. In fact, in the year of trial was held, the racial balance could have gone anywhere from 0% to 57% minority in the Seattle schools and still been within the Seattle schools' definition. Do you agree with the Attorney General's proposition that the state's authority supersedes all the local authority of the local school board? We believe we agree with that proposition as a general matter. Certainly, the state is entirely free to structure its political processes in just about any way it chooses to do so, except in a way that violates the Equal Protection Clause by establishing a racial classification or by adopting a statute at least in part because of discriminatory intent. Both courts were correct. Mr. Togue, before you go ahead, absent de gire segregation, is there any legal duty at all to auto busing? Under the federal constitution, there is not a constitutional duty to require busing in absence of de gire segregation. However, the record in this case shows that the Seattle School Board had a good faith belief that their failure to take action to desegregate the schools in response to threats of litigation over desegregation would necessarily involve them in federal court control and running of the school system. That decision was made only after 15 years of unsuccessful efforts to desegregate the schools by all possible voluntary means. Has there ever been any finding of de gire violation in the state of Washington? As applied to a school system and its student assignment policies, no. Nevertheless, this statute at issue in this case establishes a racial classification, as both courts below found, that is in no material respect any different from those in Hunter v. Erickson and Lee v. Nyquist. The initiative was designed to and does prohibit assignments beyond nearby schools, only in the case of racial desegregation. It permits all the traditional assignments away from nearby schools that went on in the state of Washington before the initiative was adopted. And further, as this court knows from its own experience, Section 3 of the initiative, which prohibits school districts indirectly from violating the nearest or next-nearest school rule, is simply a list of the common desegregation techniques which the federal courts of this country have ordered for 30 years. In short, race is written all over the face of Initiative 350, even though the word race and the word desegregation never appear by design. This court, however, need not decide whether the presumption of unconstitutional purpose, which arises with a racial classification, invalidates the statute in this case, because plaintiffs established at trial, the trial court found, on the basis of much evidence, that a discriminatory purpose was a factor in the adoption of Initiative 350. But the Court of Appeals didn't pass on that finding, did it? The Court of Appeals found it unnecessary to reach that finding because of its ruling on the racial classification ground. So if you were to rely on, if you were to suggest that that is available to you here, might not the normal course of events be for us to remand it to the Court of Appeals for passing on, reviewing that finding? If the court does not agree with the Court of Appeals that a racial classification was established, that is one course open to the court, certainly. However, the evidence that I will review ought to satisfy the court. I think that a racially discriminatory purpose, and in fact racial bias, was among the reasons for this Initiative's adoption. This court reviews the legal validity of the Court of Appeals judgment. It does not have to agree with the reasoning of the Court of Appeals to affirm the judgment. Mr. Hoagie, you've used the term, as did the Court of Appeals, racial classification. Would you tell me who the members are of the respective classes that the statute differentiates between? The statute differentiates between the majority, the white community, and the minority community, in its treatment of reasons for assigning students away from their neighborhood schools. Prior to enactment of the initiative, Washington had a policy permitting and, in fact, encouraging the assignment of students away from neighborhood schools for the purpose of desegregation. It regulated student assignment, not at all. That was entirely within the discretion of local school districts. After the initiative, all traditional reasons for assigning students away from their neighborhood schools is preserved, except for the reason of assigning... Is this a classification of reasons that are in a permissible and an impermissible category, or is it a classification of two classes of persons? It's a classification of two classes of persons, as was the statute in country versus ericsson, because... Now, who's in the favored class and who's in the disfavored class? The statute favors the majority, the white majority. The protected class, for purposes of the 14th Amendment analysis, is minority people who have an interest in equitable, desegregated education. That political and educational interest is the only one that Initiative 350 affects. Initiative 350 permits school districts to assign students away from their neighborhood schools. For all reasons that exist and that school districts commonly use, that was the finding of the district court. Initiative 350 does not, however, allow the minority interest in desegregated education to be satisfied through the local political process. It removes only that discretion from local school authorities. Are you telling us that the Initiative 350 has resulted in a dual school system again? Initiative 350, if applied in the state of Washington, would resegregate the schools and would, therefore... Has it done so in Seattle? The Initiative has not been applied in Seattle because its operation has been enjoined pending this hearing. If it is applied as it is defined, how will it produce a dual school system? Can you give us that factually? Yes. The court below found, and the Court of Appeals agreed, that it would be impossible to achieve any significant racial desegregation in Seattle. It would be impossible, in fact, to desegregate the Tacoma and Pasco school systems as well, without resort to the tools of desegregation which are specifically prohibited by Section 3 of the Initiative. In fact, the condition of segregation in Seattle after Initiative 350 would be more dramatic, more drastic segregation than has ever existed before, partly because the successful mandatory middle school program, which had been operating for six years, would be disestablished, also because, as the District Court found, white parents would continue, under Initiative 350, to move away from minority residential areas or transition areas and thereby increase residential segregation and increase school segregation. Moreover, blacks in Seattle, the testimony showed and the Court found, would take the white community's repudiation of equitable desegregation as expressed in Initiative 350 as a sign that they should no longer continue their historic support for voluntary efforts and would themselves withdraw into their neighborhood schools. Supposing that the school board had adopted precisely the policy that's contained in Initiative 350, would you say that the school board was guilty of making a racial classification? If the school board continued to assign students away from their neighborhood schools for all the reasons the initiative allows, that policy, if it was continued, would not amount to any change in Washington's or the Seattle School District's former history, and so it would not be an establishment of a racial classification. If the decision were made to rescind the Seattle plan, that would still be by reference to the neutral principles that are approved under Hunter v. Erickson. The decision whether to rescind the Seattle plan and the validity of that decision would depend on whether there was a de-jury segregation condition that has to be remedied or whether the decision was made with a discriminatory purpose, as the Court specifically found was true with reference to Initiative 350. But absent such a finding, you wouldn't say that the school board was making an independently unconstitutional racial classification simply by adhering to the policy contained in Initiative 350. It would partly depend on whether there was a rescission of an operating desegregation plan, as this Court unanimously pointed out in Dayton 1. But continuing a former policy of assigning to neighborhood schools with the exceptions of Initiative 350 wouldn't be a racial classification. But it becomes a racial classification simply because it's done at the state level rather than the school board level? Part of the reason the ordinance in Hunter v. Erickson was invalidated and the statute in Lee v. Snyquist was invalidated was that it singled out for a decision at a different level of government only that part of student assignment authority or housing matter authority, which was of interest to the minority. Well, Hunter simply made any ordinance pertaining to the sale of property or anti-discrimination ordinance subject to a referendum where nothing else was subject to a referendum, isn't it? All matters under the Akron housing law were subject to ordinance. The peculiar or subject to local referendum, any statute or ordinance passed by the city council could be subjected to referendum.
